article.overview: The catalogue name describes a function rather than one standard instrument. A regolith compaction tester would characterise how densely lunar regolith is packed, or how it responds when compacted, so that engineers can judge whether the ground can support landers, habitats, roads and landing pads. No flown lunar instrument with this exact name was identified in the sources reviewed. The closest flown precedent is the Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer (SRP), which measured how hard the soil resisted a probe pushed into it. The closest modern work is a compaction device tested only on Earth in lunar simulant.
article.description: A regolith compaction tester is best understood as a family of possible designs rather than a single product. Two broad approaches appear in the sources reviewed. The first is penetration-based testing, in which a probe, cone or plate is pushed into the ground while force and depth are recorded; the force-depth curve is then interpreted to estimate soil strength and density. This is the approach used by the Apollo SRP. The second is active compaction, in which a device compacts the surface with a plate, roller or actuator and its effect on the regolith is measured. Ground-based work of this type uses lunar simulants such as GreenSpar-250 (a lunar Highlands analogue) and AGK-2010 (a lunar Mare analogue), and University of Adelaide research uses a 1:13 scale roller model on a lunar highlands simulant. Neither approach has been shown in the sources reviewed to be a flight-qualified regolith compaction tester.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Regolith density and strength control how the ground behaves under load. Measurements of these properties are relevant to foundations and load-bearing surfaces for landers, habitats and rovers; to preparation of landing and launch pads, roads and berms, where compaction may be a construction step; and to understanding the mechanical history of the lunar surface and the relationship between density and strength. The Apollo penetrometer experiments were designed for this kind of information. The Apollo 15 PDS record describes the penetrometer as part of the Apollo soil mechanics investigation, and the NASA Apollo 16 page states that the analysis method is intended to estimate soil properties from penetration force using soil mechanics theory and model tests.
article.operating_principle: Penetrometer principle (Apollo SRP): the SRP has a reference pad that rests on the surface and a shaft carrying interchangeable tips. Penetration depth is measured by a retractor cable linked to the reference pad, which moves a stylus along a recording drum. Applied force deflects a calibrated coil spring, which rotates the drum in proportion to force. The recording head is removed after the test and returned to Earth, where the etched record is read. The soil-strength interpretation depends on a soil-to-penetrometer friction ratio, which the Apollo 16 analysis takes as 0.5, and the same analysis notes that one measurement cannot uniquely determine both cohesion and friction angle. Compaction principle (ESA-funded breadboard): the Astronika compaction device uses a high-energy voice coil actuator that drives a baseplate into the regolith at varying frequencies and strokes, densifying the material. The project report and related summaries describe improved surface geotechnical properties in both simulants; numerical results were not available in the sources read.
article.scientific_importance: Soil strength and density are central inputs to lunar engineering and to the study of regolith evolution. The Apollo SRP provided some of the first in-situ penetration data on the lunar surface [2]. Modern compaction work matters because it tests whether regolith can be prepared for infrastructure without importing dense ground materials from Earth. Both strands remain limited by the fact that most modern compaction evidence is from simulants, and that the vacuum and low-gravity behaviour of real regolith is not fully characterised [4][6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a regolith compaction tester. The values below apply only to the named instruments and sources.

examples.name: Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer (SRP / LSRP)
examples.type: Historical lunar instrument (flown on Apollo 15 and Apollo 16)
examples.mass_note: 2.3 kg per the Apollo 15 PDS instrument record. The Apollo 16 page does not state a mass.

max_recordable_force_n.note: The sources read do not explain the difference between the two flights.

examples.recording_method: Recording drum in the upper canister; force deflects a calibrated coil spring which rotates the drum; the recording head is returned to Earth after the test.
examples.power_consumption_w: Not described in the pages read; recording mechanism described as spring-driven and mechanical.
examples.dimensions: Overall dimensions not stated in the pages read.
examples.tests_flown: Apollo 15: four cone penetration tests and two plate-load tests near the ALSEP site. Apollo 16: test sites not stated on the page read; search summaries refer to Station 4 and Station 10 (not verified).
examples.soil_property_estimates_unverified: Search summaries (not read directly) report a friction angle of about 35 to 40 degrees and in-place density of about 1.5 to 2.0 g/cm3 for Apollo 15, and surface cohesion of about 0.1 to 1.0 kN/m2 with friction angles of about 30 to 50 degrees for Apollo 16. These must be checked against the primary NASA chapters before reuse.
examples.qualification: Flown Apollo-era hardware. Interpretation depends on a soil-to-penetrometer friction ratio assumed as 0.5 in the Apollo 16 analysis.

examples.name: ESA-funded regolith compaction breadboard (Astronika)
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.actuator: High-energy voice coil actuator that drives a baseplate into the regolith at varying frequencies and strokes.
examples.simulant_result_note: Compaction was deeper and more forceful in AGK-2010, which the project attributes mainly to its wider particle size distribution. Numerical results were not available in the sources read.
examples.project_status: Described as closed, with an 18-month duration and a budget of 175,000 EUR (search summary citing ESA activities page; not read directly).
examples.trl: TRL 4 for the current improved design, per an Astronika paper summarised in search results. An earlier summary cites TRL 4 in late 2022. Not verified in a primary document read.
examples.test_bed_size_conflict: An IAC abstract cites more than 1,200 kg of lunar analogue; the Astronika project page describes a 1.5-tonne sandbox. Unresolved.
examples.qualification: Ground-tested breadboard in simulant. Vacuum and thermal behaviour not yet established in the project as summarised.

examples.name: University of Adelaide 1:13 scale roller studies
examples.dimensions: 1:13 scale model; full dimensions not given in the abstract read.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.result_note: The preprint abstract states that density and settlement were measured but gives no numerical values in the text read. A search summary also describes a vibrating drum roller that outperformed an impact roller in settlement and density; not confirmed from the full text.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo SRP was a hand-operated penetrometer with a long shaft, a bearing plate of 2.54 cm by 12.7 cm and interchangeable 30-degree cones; its overall dimensions are not stated in the pages read. The ESA-funded breadboard and the Adelaide roller models have no verified full-scale dimensions in the sources read. Because these examples differ in purpose, scale and maturity, they should not be treated as directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Apollo 15 PDS record gives 2.3 kg for the SRP. Mass for the Apollo 16 SRP is not stated in the page read. Mass for the ESA-funded breadboard is not publicly specified in the sources accessed. A flight regolith compaction tester would need its mass determined by its design and mounting requirements.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No electrical power requirement is described for the Apollo SRP in the pages read; its recording mechanism is described as spring-driven and mechanical. Power for the ESA-funded breadboard actuator is not publicly specified in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Verified information on how a compaction tester performs in vacuum, at lunar temperature extremes or in low gravity was not found in the sources read. The Apollo SRP was operated by astronauts at the surface, with manual indexing of each run; its environmental tolerance is not described in the pages read. For the ESA-funded breadboard, vacuum and thermal behaviour had not been tested in the project as summarised, and further lunar-specific development was proposed. The Adelaide preprint uses dry material and does not address vacuum, thermal or low-gravity conditions in the abstract. A flight instrument would need its own environmental requirements, which are not established here.
article.limitations: Penetration tests measure resistance to penetration; converting that resistance into compaction state or density depends on assumptions about friction, cohesion and soil behaviour. The Apollo SRP recorded to 76 cm and was limited by its force range. Apollo SRP results depend on the recording head being returned to Earth. Compaction results so far are from simulants, which may not reproduce the grain shape, cohesion or vacuum behaviour of real regolith. The sandbox size and some performance figures for the ESA-funded breadboard are inconsistent across sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: This is a surface payload. No flight integration is described for a regolith compaction tester in the sources reviewed. For the Apollo SRP, the instrument was carried to the surface and deployed by astronauts as part of the Apollo surface experiment programme. Stowage on the lunar module and any lander interface are not described in the pages read.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a lander or rover payload on Earth (not described for this payload in the sources reviewed).
Launch and transfer to the Moon (not described for this payload in the sources reviewed).
Deliver to the surface by a lander, or carry and deploy by astronauts (Apollo SRP precedent).

Position the instrument on the regolith and connect any required driving system, reaction support and power (ESA-funded breadboard requirements are implied by its design but not stated in the sources).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: A penetrometer requires a reference surface and a controlled push; the Apollo SRP used an astronaut-held reference pad and manual indexing. A compaction device requires a driving system, reaction support and power; for the ESA-funded breadboard, the sources do not state a lander interface, power budget or mounting method.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 15 and 16 SRPs were astronaut-operated as part of the Apollo soil mechanics investigation. On Apollo 15, four cone penetration tests and two plate-load tests were made near the ALSEP site.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified as compatible with a regolith compaction tester. Compatibility would need to be assessed against mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, power, data interfaces and thermal requirements once a specific design is defined.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 15 and 16 penetrometers were part of the Apollo soil mechanics investigation and contributed to early estimates of lunar soil strength. Apollo 15 tests were made near the ALSEP site; Apollo 16 test sites are reported in search summaries as Station 4 and Station 10 but were not stated on the page read. Modern compaction work has continued through ESA-funded breadboard development and University of Adelaide studies in simulant. None of these has been shown to fly.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flown instrument with the exact catalogue name was identified. Apollo soil-property numbers come from search summaries and must be checked against primary NASA chapters. The Apollo SRP analysis assumed a friction ratio of 0.5 and cannot uniquely determine both cohesion and friction angle from one measurement. A 2023 Lunar and Planetary Science Conference abstract argues that Apollo-era friction estimates ignored depth and that friction and cohesion increase with depth; it is model-based, was not read in full and is not treated as established. Mass, dimensions, power, vacuum and thermal behaviour and lunar TRL for the compactor are not verified in primary sources read. Several sources were not read in full (redirects, 403, 404 or search summary only) and are flagged in the references.

data_quality_notes: No flown lunar instrument with the exact name 'Regolith compaction tester' was identified in the sources reviewed; the article treats the name as a functional category.
Apollo SRP maximum recordable force differs between sources: 111 N (Apollo 15 PDS record) and 215 N (Apollo 16 page). The reason is not stated in the pages read.
Apollo SRP mass of 2.3 kg is from the Apollo 15 PDS record; the Apollo 16 mass is not stated.
Apollo soil-property estimates (friction angle, density, cohesion) are from search summaries of NASA Apollo chapters that were not fetched (R7, R8) and must be verified before reuse.
ESA-funded compactor data (TRL 4, 18-month duration, 175,000 EUR budget) come from search summaries; the ESA activity page returned 403 and the ESA report redirected.
Test-bed size conflict for the Astronika breadboard: over 1,200 kg (IAC abstract) versus 1.5 tonnes (Astronika page). Unresolved.
The 2023 LPSC abstract (R9) on depth-dependent friction is model-based and was not read in full; it is not treated as established.
The 2026 EngrXiv preprint (R3) is by Brendan Scott and colleagues at the University of Adelaide and is not the same person as the Apollo-era R.F. Scott.
No images were verified in this run; image arrays are empty and research_status image fields are false.
Vacuum, thermal and low-gravity performance of any compaction device has not been verified from primary sources.
